analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $35 a month for privately insured patients and helps uninsured diabetics get insulin.
analysis.headline: A one-senator bill to cap insulin out-of-pocket costs at $35 a month has sat untouched in a Senate committee since May 2026, with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap what people with private health insurance pay out of pocket for insulin at the lesser of $35 or 25% of the insulin's net price per 30-day supply, with no deductible applied to those products [S2][S3]. It would also set up a federal program in which pharmacies and health care providers sell insulin to uninsured people, with the government reimbursing providers for the difference between the patient's cost and $35 [S2][S3]. It does not lower insulin list prices or address Medicare, which already caps insulin copays under a 2022 law.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who use insulin would pay at most $35 (or 25% of the drug's net price, whichever is less) for a 30-day supply, with no deductible standing between them and their insulin, including on high-deductible and catastrophic plans [S3]. Uninsured people who need insulin could get it from participating pharmacies and providers for $35 a month, and could not be billed for more [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured insulin users and uninsured diabetics

how_it_helps.text: Caps cost-sharing for a 30-day supply of covered insulin at the lesser of $35 or 25% of the drug's negotiated net price, and bars plans from applying a deductible to those insulin products, starting in plan year 2027.

Requires plans to cover at least one insulin of every type (rapid-, short-, intermediate-, long-, ultra long-acting, and premixed) and dosage form (vial, pump, or inhaler), and makes catastrophic plans cover those products before the annual out-of-pocket limit is met.

Creates a program under which the Department of Health and Human Services pays pharmacies and health care providers the difference between what an uninsured patient would otherwise pay for a 30-day insulin supply and $35, and participating providers cannot hold the patient liable for the rest.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor plans would absorb the cost of insulin that previously counted toward deductibles and cost-sharing, which could show up as higher premiums [S3]. Federal taxpayers would fund the new uninsured-insulin program; the bill contains no funding source, and Congress included a statement that a future bill should offset the federal costs [S3]. Pharmacies and providers would front the discount and then be reimbursed by HHS [S2]. Insulin list prices themselves are left untouched [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill is unpaid for: it creates federal spending on the uninsured-insulin program without identifying any offset, and states only that Congress 'should' pass an offset later.

It caps what patients pay, not what insulin costs. List prices are untouched, so the savings come from insurers and employers and could be passed back to consumers through higher premiums rather than through lower drug prices.

The protection is narrower than it sounds: plans choose which insulin products count as 'selected', the cap applies only to in-network dispensing, and plans may still charge more for other insulin products.
It applies only to private insurance and the uninsured; it does nothing about Medicare, where insulin copays were already capped by a 2022 law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insulin users the benefit is real and immediate: a hard $35 monthly ceiling with no deductible is a genuine protection for people who can otherwise face hundreds of dollars in early-year costs. But the design is modest and arguably expensive: it leaves the underlying price of insulin alone, shifts costs onto premiums and the federal budget, and explicitly defers paying for the uninsured program to a future bill. A stronger version would have attacked list prices or required offsets up front.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2026 and sent to the Senate's health committee, which has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Senator John Kennedy introduced the bill in the Senate on May 13, 2026.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the bill has zero cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further action of any kind since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no patient has gained anything: insulin users keep paying today's prices while insurers, employers, and insulin makers keep the existing arrangements. The bill is still technically alive, but with no cosponsors and no committee action, it is drifting toward dying quietly when this Congress ends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and insulin makers keep status quo

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 13, 2026 and is its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 13, 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senators signed on as cosponsors, so there is no record showing whether support or opposition would split by party; the bill's only sponsor is a Republican.

industries.note: The bill forces private plans to cover selected insulin without a deductible and cap patient cost-sharing at $35 a month, costs the industry currently shifts to patients. Insurers would likely recover some of this through higher premiums, so part of the burden lands back on the public.

The bill caps what patients pay but never touches insulin list prices, and the new federal program for uninsured people pays providers based on the drug's prevailing cost — meaning the government reimburses at today's high prices. Manufacturers keep their pricing power while the public picks up more of the bill.

Participating pharmacies and providers get guaranteed $35-per-month insulin sales from insured patients and full reimbursement from HHS for the discount they give uninsured patients. Their financial interest here lines up with the patient's.

The $35-or-25% cap is calculated from the insulin's price net of all concessions, including rebates pocketed by middlemen like PBMs, implicitly building their rebate system into the law rather than reforming it.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action, and roughly two months left in this Congress, the bill is very unlikely to move on its own. Its realistic paths are to die quietly at the end of the session or to have its provisions folded into a larger health package — neither of which has any visible support right now.
